v.why: Pooling is often thought harmless as a cheap mixer, but in strong parents (conv on the first edge) it destroys more accuracy, while weak parents sit near the floor and lose little.
The substitute story predicts edge 5's conv cushions the loss, but strong parents have more to lose, so the harm from swapping in pooling is larger there.
Pooling might seem a reasonable placeholder, but it is among the weakest ops on the final edge, so upgrading it to conv yields an above-average gain.
Pooling and skip both seem like parameter-free ops of similar value, but replacing the residual skip with pooling removes a clean gradient path, so the edit hurts more than when it replaces none.
Adding skips is often thought to ease optimization, but a second skip into the output pushes the cell toward the shallow, skip-dominated regime known to perform poorly, so the edit is worse here.
Removing the deep 1-to-2 edge seems costly, but when node 2 already gets a strong conv input from edge 1 the redundancy makes the loss smaller.
One might think a cheap conv on edge 5 complements a direct conv, but parents with a 3x3 on edge 3 are already strong, so headroom shrinks the gain.
A second conv into the output from a different source seems to add diversity, but saturation means the gain is smaller once one strong conv already reaches the output.
Adding a conv to the first hop seems to deepen the network regardless, but a parent already convolving the input on edge 1 has less headroom, so the gain saturates.
A direct input-to-output conv looks like it adds a new path, but parents with a conv on edge 5 are already strong, so the improvement is compressed by headroom.
